conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is well supported by evidence and concludes that 'the claim is true, not false,' citing multiple randomized controlled trials and FDA approval. Therefore, it endorses the claim.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
The claim is well supported by evidence — it is not false.

The pivotal study is a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine (Devinsky et al., 2017), which enrolled 120 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome and drug-resistant seizures. Add-on cannabidiol (CBD) significantly reduced convulsive seizure frequency compared with placebo over a 14-week period, though it was associated with adverse effects such as diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618).

This finding was replicated in a subsequent dose-ranging randomized trial (JAMA Neurology, 2020), which tested two CBD doses against placebo and found both significantly reduced convulsive seizure frequency in treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458).

Long-term open-label extension data further support durability of effect: a study in Epilepsia (2018) reported that long-term CBD treatment had an acceptable safety profile and led to sustained, clinically meaningful reductions in seizure frequency (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/epi.14628).

Based on this cumulative randomized-trial evidence, the U.S. FDA approved Epidiolex (pharmaceutical-grade CBD) specifically as an add-on treatment for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome (as well as Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex) — the first cannabis-derived drug ever approved by the agency (https://www.drugs.com/history/epidiolex.html).

**Conclusion:** The claim is true, not false. Multiple independent randomized controlled trials and regulatory review confirm that add-on CBD reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children with Dravet syndrome, though it carries known side effects requiring monitoring.
